I can only speak to personal experience starting in the late 80s, but a history of scholarship of several fields suggest mini revolutions in language and perception going back into the 60s and beyond.

In the early 80s, and finally reaching a head in the early 90s, was the idea of 'politically correct' speech (when the term was first coined). People were flipping out over the way professors would talk about anybody that was 'other' if they didn't use proper and cautious language. It got very silly. I was in a class where we were discussing the Aztecs, and human sacrifice was part of the discussion. One student raised her hand and asked why we always love to talk about human sacrifice among peoples that aren't Western European, but that every time evidence pops up for human sacrifice in Europe, the skeptics shoot down the evidence in an effort to preserve european heritage. Those incidents happened quite frequently, and professors thought a lot about their words before speaking. When that tempest mellowed out, it mellowed out fast. And the end result was that people were more cautious in the way they phrased things, but speech and understanding were in no way stifled.

In the late 90s and early 2000s, the work of Martin Bernal blew up in popularity, in which he suggested that Greek culture (and hence all of Western civ) owed all of its trappings to Africa. That Africans colonized Greece, and that all got white-washed in the 18th century. And that the ancient Egyptians were black Africans and not of Middle-Eastern origin. This resulted in complaints about western civ teaching methods nationwide. People were refusing to even touch the class because you'd have formal complaints filed against you if you didn't offer the popular doctrine.

And from before my time, there were some major revolutions in the late 60s and early 70s, particularly in the acknowledgement of value judgments in the teaching of 'primitive' or 'savage' cultures. No doubt there are others that I'm not aware of.

But the pattern is almost always the same. A new social perspective arises. A passionate group realizes that this perspective has been ignored. They push back fanatically against the established doctrine. Another equally passionate group pushes back and says things are fine the way they are and people need to stop being butthurt. Passions die down, and in the end we have some reasonable and rational new perspectives that make study more interesting. In the wake of Bernal, civ courses really did start to focus on (legitimate) global interconnections that had been ignored in favor of a simplified narrative. And the study of ethnicity and identity blew up all over the place, which has been of tremendous value for historical studies. The fights of the 70s resulted in more thoughtful anthropological study, which has allowed for huge inroads in observing and assessing social interactions from any period and region. The early 90s PC movement resulted in ignored populations being introduced into the mainstream dialogue and discussion.

It all levels out eventually. I think that those changes can't happen without abrasive characters acting unreasonable first.
